decks.title: Index Numbers — Part 1: Meaning, Types and Uses
goals: Define an index number and the base period
Explain the wholesale price index, the consumer price index, the index of industrial production and the Sensex
State the uses of index numbers and the issues in constructing one
Read an index and deflate a money value to real terms

slides.heading: Index Numbers
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how we **measure change** in prices and output against a **base period**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what an index number is, the base period, the wholesale price index, the consumer price index and the index of industrial production, uses, and issues in construction
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Prices change, output changes, and we want one number that shows how much. That number is an index. In this part we learn what an index number is, why a base period matters, and what the wholesale price index, the consumer price index and the index of industrial production measure. All the data are imagined.

slides.heading: What is an index number?
slides.body_md: An **index number** is a statistical device that measures the **relative change** in a variable, or a group of related variables, over time, compared with a **base period** taken as **100**.

visual.alt: Table of an imagined notebook price in Bhavnagar Colony, Year 0 Rs 40, Year 1 Rs 50, Year 2 Rs 36, and its index with Year 0 as the base: 100, 125, 90
visual.caption: Imagined notebook price. Index = price ÷ base price × 100.

slides.narration: An index number measures how much something has changed compared with a starting period called the base. Look at an imagined notebook in Bhavnagar Colony. In the base year it costs 40 rupees, and the index is 100. When the price becomes 50 rupees, the index is 125. When it falls to 36 rupees, the index is 90.

slides.heading: The base period
slides.body_md: The base period is the **reference** for comparison. It should be a **normal year**, free of abnormal events.

rows: The same as the base period
Higher than the base: 25 per cent higher
Lower than the base: 10 per cent lower

visual.alt: Table reading index values against the base of 100: exactly 100 is the same as the base, 125 is 25 per cent higher, 90 is 10 per cent lower
visual.caption: Imagined notebook price from the previous table.

slides.narration: The base period is the yardstick. Its index is always 100. An index above 100 means higher than the base, and an index below 100 means lower. An index of 125 shows a rise of 25 per cent, and 90 shows a fall of 10 per cent. A good base year is a normal one, without a shortage or a flood.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading an index
slides.body_md: A retail price index is 125 against a base of 100. What does this show?
slides.narration: Remember that the base is 100. Ask by how many points the index is above the base, and what share of the base that is. Then choose the option that states the rise correctly as a per cent.

slides.heading: Wholesale price index
slides.body_md: The **wholesale price index** measures the change in the general price level of goods **traded in bulk**.

rows: Change in the general price level of goods traded in bulk
Office of the Economic Adviser, Ministry of Commerce and Industry
Follow price movements in bulk markets and in the cost of inputs

visual.alt: Table of the wholesale price index: what it measures, the prices used, who compiles it as commonly taught, and what it is used for

slides.narration: The wholesale price index follows the prices at which goods are traded in bulk, not the prices in a shop. As commonly taught, it is compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser in the Ministry of Commerce and Industry. It helps us follow price movements in bulk markets and in the cost of inputs.

slides.heading: Consumer price index
slides.body_md: The **consumer price index**, or **cost-of-living index**, measures the change in the **retail prices** of a **fixed basket** of goods and services consumed by a **defined group**.

rows: Rural households, urban households, and both together

visual.alt: Table of the kinds of consumer price index: for industrial workers, for agricultural labourers, and rural, urban and combined, with the group each follows and the compiler as commonly taught
visual.caption: Each follows the retail prices of a fixed basket consumed by its own group.

slides.narration: The consumer price index follows the retail prices of a fixed basket of goods and services bought by a defined group. As commonly taught, there are indices for industrial workers, for agricultural labourers, and for rural, urban and combined households. The first two are compiled by the Labour Bureau and the last by the national statistical office.

slides.heading: The consumer price index at work
slides.body_md: Because it follows what a group pays in shops, it is used to **adjust wages and dearness allowance**.

nodes.label: Retail prices of the basket rise
Cost of living of the group is higher

visual.alt: Flow showing how a consumer price index is used: retail prices of the basket rise, the index rises, the cost of living of the group is higher, the dearness allowance is revised, and the real wage is protected
visual.caption: The consumer price index at work

slides.narration: When retail prices of the basket rise, the consumer price index rises. The cost of living of the group is then higher. An employer can revise the dearness allowance in line with the index, so that the real wage of workers is protected. This is one of the most important uses of the consumer price index.

slides.heading: Quick check: which prices?
slides.body_md: Decide whether the statement about the wholesale price index is true or false.
slides.narration: Think about the word wholesale. Does it mean goods sold in bulk to traders, or goods sold one at a time to households at a corner shop? Then decide whether the statement is true or false.

slides.heading: Index of industrial production
slides.body_md: The **index of industrial production** measures the change in the **volume of industrial output**: mining, manufacturing and electricity.

rows: Change in the volume of industrial output
A quantity index, not a price index
The national statistical office, Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation

visual.alt: Table of the index of industrial production: what it measures, what it covers, that it is a quantity index, and who compiles it as commonly taught

slides.narration: The index of industrial production is different. It does not follow prices. It follows the volume of what industries produce, such as mining, manufacturing and electricity. It is therefore a quantity index. As commonly taught, it is compiled by the national statistical office under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: an output index
slides.body_md: The imagined Rivergate Industrial Estate has three kinds of output. Find its output index.
bullets: **Step 2 —** Multiply by the weights 20, 60, 20 and add: ΣRW = **12100**.

visual.alt: Working table for the imagined Rivergate Industrial Estate: relatives 105, 120, 140, weights 20, 60, 20, products total 12100, index 121
visual.caption: Imagined Rivergate Industrial Estate. Units of output are imagined.

slides.narration: For each kind of output we divide this year's volume by the base volume, which gives relatives of 105, 120, 140. We multiply each by its weight and add, which gives 12100. Dividing by the total weight of 100 gives an index of 121. Output is 21 per cent above the base.

slides.heading: The Sensex and the four indices compared
slides.body_md: The **Sensex** is the stock market index of the **Bombay Stock Exchange**, based on the share prices of **30 companies**.

rows: Prices of goods traded in bulk
Retail prices of a fixed basket of a defined group
Volume of output of mining, manufacturing and electricity
Share prices of thirty companies on the Bombay Stock Exchange

visual.alt: Table comparing the wholesale price index, the consumer price index, the index of industrial production and the Sensex by what each measures and its kind

slides.narration: The Sensex is the stock market index of the Bombay Stock Exchange. It follows the share prices of thirty companies. So we now have four indices. The wholesale price index follows bulk prices. The consumer price index follows retail prices of a basket. The index of industrial production follows volume. The Sensex follows share prices.

slides.heading: Quick check: match the index
slides.body_md: Match each index with what it measures.
slides.narration: Go through each index one at a time. Ask whether it follows bulk prices, retail prices of a basket, the volume of output, or share prices. Then pair it with the matching description.

slides.heading: Uses of index numbers
slides.body_md: Index numbers help us **measure inflation**, **adjust wages**, **deflate values**, **make policy** and **compare performance**.

rows: The colony index rises from one year to the next
A mill revises dearness allowance when the index rises
A printer compares sales at base-year prices
Planners watch price and output indices
An output index shows whether an estate has grown

visual.alt: Table of the uses of index numbers: measuring inflation, adjusting wages and allowances, deflating values to real terms, policy-making, and comparing performance over time, each with an imagined illustration

slides.narration: Index numbers have many uses. They measure inflation. They adjust wages and allowances. They deflate money values to real terms. Policy makers watch them, and they let us compare performance over time. In each case the index gives one clear number for a change that would otherwise be hard to describe.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: deflating to real terms
slides.body_md: The imagined Kaushal Printers had rising sales. Remove the effect of rising prices.
bullets: Sales grew by **37.28** per cent in money terms but only **20** per cent in real terms.

visual.alt: Working table for the imagined Kaushal Printers: sales 250, 286, 343.2 deflated by the index 125, 130, 143 give real sales 200, 220, 240
visual.caption: Imagined Kaushal Printers. Real sales = sales ÷ index × 100.

slides.narration: Money sales rose from 250 to 343.2 lakh rupees, which looks like growth of 37.28 per cent. But prices also rose. Dividing each sale by the index and multiplying by 100 gives real sales of 200, 220 and 240. The real growth is only 20 per cent. Deflating shows how much of the rise was real.

slides.heading: Issues in constructing an index
slides.body_md: Six questions must be settled before an index is built.

rows: What is to be measured, and for whom?
Is it a normal year, free of abnormal events?
Which goods and services should be included?
Are wholesale or retail prices to be used?
Which method of combining the prices is suitable?

visual.alt: Table of the six issues in constructing an index number: purpose, base year, items, price quotations, weights and formula, each with the question to settle

slides.narration: Before building an index we settle six issues. What is the purpose? Which base year? Which items? Are prices wholesale or retail? What weights should the items carry? And which formula will combine the prices? A weak answer to any of these can make the index misleading for its purpose.

slides.heading: Choosing the right index for the job
slides.body_md: The **purpose** decides the index: match the job to what the index measures.

rows: Revise the dearness allowance of a mill
Study the price movement of bulk grain
Check whether a factory's output has risen
Follow the general movement of share prices

visual.alt: Table pairing four jobs with the suitable index: dearness allowance with the consumer price index, bulk grain prices with the wholesale price index, factory output with the index of industrial production, and share prices with the Sensex

slides.narration: The purpose decides the index. To revise the dearness allowance of a mill we use the consumer price index. To study bulk grain prices we use the wholesale price index. To check whether a factory has produced more we use the index of industrial production. To follow the share market we use the Sensex.

slides.heading: Quick check: which is a use?
slides.body_md: Which of these is not a use of index numbers?
slides.narration: Recall the standard uses: measuring inflation, adjusting wages, deflating values, policy and comparison. An index shows change over time. Find the option that asks an index to do something else.

slides.narration: To recap. An index number measures relative change against a base period taken as 100. slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Define an index number with the **base period taken as 100**.
Say clearly whether an index measures **prices or volume**.
Name the **group** whose basket a consumer price index follows.
List the issues: **purpose, base year, items, price quotations, weights, formula**.
When deflating, **divide by the index and multiply by 100**.
slides.narration: Some tips. Define an index number with the base period taken as one hundred. Say clearly whether an index measures prices or volume. Name the group whose basket a consumer price index follows. List the six issues in construction. And when you deflate a money value, divide by the index and multiply by one hundred.

decks.title: Index Numbers — Part 2: Methods and Inflation
goals: Calculate a simple aggregative index and a simple average of price relatives
Calculate Laspeyres and Paasche indices and say what each means
Construct a consumer price index as a weighted average of price relatives
Find the rate of inflation, the real wage and the purchasing power

slides.heading: Methods and Inflation
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **building** an index, and using it to find **inflation** and the **real wage**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: simple aggregative method, price relatives, Laspeyres and Paasche, the consumer price index, and inflation and the real wage
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we build price indices by different methods. We begin with the simple aggregative method, then price relatives, then the weighted methods of Laspeyres and Paasche. Next we construct a consumer price index from a family budget. Finally we use an index to find the rate of inflation and the real wage. All data are imagined.

slides.heading: Four methods at a glance
slides.body_md: Methods differ in whether they use **weights** and whether they use **prices** or **relatives**.

visual.alt: Tree of the methods of constructing a price index: simple aggregative, simple average of price relatives, weighted aggregative with Laspeyres and Paasche, and weighted average of price relatives
visual.caption: Four methods

slides.narration: There are four methods to learn. The simple aggregative method adds up prices. The simple average of price relatives averages the relatives. The weighted aggregative methods, named after Laspeyres and Paasche, use quantities as weights. And the weighted average of price relatives uses budget weights, which is how a consumer price index is built.

slides.heading: Simple aggregative method
slides.body_md: Add the current prices and the base prices separately: **index = Σp1 ÷ Σp0 × 100**.

visual.alt: Table of the formulas: simple aggregative, simple average of relatives, Laspeyres, Paasche and weighted average of relatives
visual.caption: p0 is the base price, p1 the current price, q0 the base quantity, q1 the current quantity, R the relative and W the weight.

slides.narration: In the simple aggregative method we add up the current prices of all items, add up their base prices, divide the first total by the second and multiply by one hundred. The formulas for all the methods in this part are shown together in the table, with the symbols explained below it.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: bakery inputs
slides.body_md: The imagined Sunrise Bakery bought four inputs. Find the simple aggregative price index.

visual.alt: Table of the input prices of the imagined Sunrise Bakery: base prices 40, 40, 400, 60 total 540, current prices 44, 46, 480, 78 total 648, index 120
visual.caption: Imagined Sunrise Bakery, prices in rupees.

slides.narration: The base prices of the four inputs add up to 540 rupees. The current prices add up to 648 rupees. Dividing 648 by 540 and multiplying by one hundred gives an index of 120. So the prices of the bakery's inputs are, on this measure, 20 per cent higher than in the base year.

slides.heading: Quick check: a simple index
slides.body_md: Find the simple aggregative price index for another set of prices.
slides.narration: Add the base prices, add the current prices, divide the second total by the first, and multiply by one hundred. Keep your working in two lines, one for each total.

slides.heading: The limitation: units
slides.body_md: The sum of prices **depends on the units** in which each item is quoted. Price relatives do not.

rows: Butter per kg, eggs per dozen
Butter per 100 g, eggs per piece

visual.alt: Table comparing the imagined Sunrise Bakery index under two ways of quoting the prices: 120 and 115.6 by the simple aggregative method, but 118.75 by the average of relatives in both cases
visual.caption: The same price movements, quoted in different units.

slides.narration: Suppose the bakery quotes butter per hundred grams and eggs per piece instead of per kilogram and per dozen. The price movements are the same, yet the simple aggregative index changes from 120 to 115.6. The average of price relatives stays at 118.75 either way, because each relative is a pure ratio.

slides.heading: Price relatives
slides.body_md: A **price relative** is **p1 ÷ p0 × 100**. The simple average of the relatives is **Σ(p1 ÷ p0 × 100) ÷ n**.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: average of relatives
slides.body_md: Find the index for the Sunrise Bakery by the simple average of price relatives.

visual.alt: Working table for the imagined Sunrise Bakery: relatives 110, 115, 120, 130 total 475, so the index is 475 divided by 4, which is 118.75
visual.caption: Imagined Sunrise Bakery.

slides.narration: For each input we divide the current price by the base price and multiply by one hundred. The relatives are 110, 115, 120, 130. They add up to 475. Dividing by the number of items, which is 4, gives 118.75. This treats every input as equally important, which is a limitation.

slides.heading: Weighted aggregative methods
slides.body_md: Quantities act as **weights**. **Laspeyres** uses **base-year** quantities; **Paasche** uses **current-year** quantities.

rows: What does the base-year basket cost now, compared with then?
What does the current basket cost now, compared with its cost at base prices?

visual.alt: Table comparing the Laspeyres and Paasche methods by their weights and the question each answers

slides.narration: Weighted methods give each item an importance based on the quantity bought. The Laspeyres index uses the quantities of the base year. It asks what the old basket costs now compared with what it cost then. The Paasche index uses the quantities of the current year. It asks what the current basket costs now compared with its cost at base prices.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: stationers
slides.body_md: The imagined Pinecrest Stationers sold four items in two terms. Find the Laspeyres and Paasche indices.

visual.alt: Working table for the imagined Pinecrest Stationers: Σp0q0 500, Σp1q0 616, Σp0q1 1000, Σp1q1 1212; Laspeyres 123.2 and Paasche 121.2
visual.caption: Imagined Pinecrest Stationers. Prices in rupees, quantities in units sold.

slides.narration: We find the cost of each basket at each set of prices. The base term basket costs 500 rupees at base prices and 616 rupees at current prices, which gives a Laspeyres index of 123.2. The current term basket costs 1000 at base prices and 1212 at current prices, which gives a Paasche index of 121.2.

slides.heading: Quick check: Paasche weights
slides.body_md: True or false: the Paasche index uses the quantities of the current year as weights.
slides.narration: Recall which year supplies the quantities in each method. One of the two weighted methods uses base year quantities and the other uses current year quantities. Decide whether the statement matches the Paasche method.

slides.heading: Why Laspeyres and Paasche differ
slides.body_md: When buyers shift away from items that became **dearer**, the **Paasche** value tends to be **lower**.

visual.alt: Table of Laspeyres and Paasche indices for four imagined data sets: stationers 123.2 and 121.2, canteen 124.8 and 123.75, household 126 and 123.75, juice bar 122 and 121.25
visual.caption: In each imagined set buyers bought less of the items that became dearer, so the Paasche value is lower.

slides.narration: The two methods usually give different answers because the quantities differ. In each of these imagined sets, buyers bought less of the items that became dearer. The base year weights keep the old buying pattern, so Laspeyres is higher. The current year weights reflect the shift, so Paasche is lower. Laspeyres needs quantities only once, but Paasche needs them every year.

slides.heading: Consumer price index: weighted relatives
slides.body_md: The **consumer price index** is a **weighted average of price relatives**: **ΣRW ÷ ΣW**, with weights from the **family budget**.

Multiply each R by its weight W

slides.narration: A consumer price index is built as a weighted average of price relatives. First find the relative of each item. Then multiply each relative by its weight, taken from the family budget, which shows how much the family spends on that item. Add the products, and divide by the total of the weights.

visual.caption: Imagined Madhupur Mill Colony. Weights are base-year monthly spending of a worker family.

slides.heading: Quick check: steps of the method
slides.body_md: Put the steps of constructing a consumer price index in order.
slides.narration: Think about what each step needs. You cannot weight a relative before you have found it, and you cannot divide by the total weight before the weighted values are added. The division comes last.

slides.heading: Inflation from an index
slides.body_md: **Inflation** is a **sustained rise in the general price level**. Rate = **(I1 − I0) ÷ I0 × 100**.

visual.alt: Table of the imagined Bhavnagar Colony index 100, 125, 130, 143, 150, 165 for Years 0 to 5 with the changes 25, 5, 13, 7, 15 and the rates of inflation 25, 4, 10, 4.9, 10 per cent
visual.caption: Imagined Bhavnagar Colony. Rate = change ÷ earlier index × 100.

slides.narration: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level. From an index, the rate is the change in the index divided by the earlier index, times one hundred. In our imagined colony the rates are 25, 4, 10, 4.9, 10 per cent over the five years. Notice that a lower rate, such as 4.9 per cent, still means prices are rising, only more slowly.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: finding inflation
slides.body_md: Use the imagined Bhavnagar Colony index: Year 2 = 130, Year 3 = 143.

visual.alt: Table of the imagined Bhavnagar Colony index 100, 125, 130, 143, 150, 165 for Years 0 to 5 with the changes 25, 5, 13, 7, 15 and the rates of inflation 25, 4, 10, 4.9, 10 per cent
visual.caption: Imagined Bhavnagar Colony. Rate = change ÷ earlier index × 100.

slides.narration: From Year 2 to Year 3 the index rises from 130 to 143, a change of 13. Dividing by the earlier index of 130 and multiplying by one hundred gives 10 per cent. From Year 3 to Year 4 the change is 7, so the rate is 4.9 per cent, which is lower.

slides.heading: Quick check: a rate of inflation
slides.body_md: Find the rate of inflation between two years from the index.
slides.narration: Subtract the earlier index from the later one. Divide the change by the earlier index, and multiply by one hundred. Give the answer as a per cent.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: real wage and purchasing power
slides.body_md: A clerk of the imagined Bhavnagar Colony Cooperative Society earns a rising money wage. Is he better off?
bullets: **Year 3 —** 17160 ÷ 143 × 100 = **12000** rupees: no better off than in Year 1.

visual.alt: Working table for an imagined clerk of Bhavnagar Colony: money wages 15000, 16900, 17160, index 125, 130, 143, real wages 12000, 13000, 12000
visual.caption: Imagined clerk. Real wage = money wage ÷ index × 100.

slides.narration: The money wage rises every year, from 15000 to 17160 rupees. But the real wage, which is the money wage divided by the index times one hundred, is 12000, then 13000, then 12000. In Year 3 the clerk is no better off than in Year 1. As the index rises, a rupee buys less, so purchasing power falls.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: p1 ÷ p0 × 100; free of units; simple average gives equal importance
Weights are base-year and current-year quantities

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: simple aggregative, price relatives, Laspeyres and Paasche, the consumer price index, the inflation rate and the real wage

slides.narration: To recap. The simple aggregative index adds up prices and depends on units. Price relatives are free of units. Laspeyres uses base year quantities and Paasche uses current year quantities. The consumer price index is a weighted average of relatives with family budget weights. Inflation is the change in the index over the earlier index, and the real wage is the money wage divided by the index times one hundred.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write the **formula first**, then substitute and show each total.
For Laspeyres use **base-year quantities**; for Paasche **current-year quantities**.
For a consumer price index, show **R, W and RW** in a table, then divide by **ΣW**.
For inflation, divide the change by the **earlier** index.
Finish with a **sentence**: prices rose by so many per cent, or the real wage fell.

sections.heading: 1. Meaning of an index number and the base period
sections.body_md:
An **index number** is a statistical device that measures the **relative change** in a variable, or a group of related variables, over time, compared with a **base period** taken as **100**. An index above 100 shows a rise over the base and an index below 100 a fall.

The **base period** should be a **normal** one, free of abnormal events such as a long shortage. Imagined example: a notebook costs Rs 40 in the base year, Rs 50 in Year 1 and Rs 36 in Year 2, so its index is 100, 125 and 90.

key_terms.definition_md: A statistical device that measures the relative change in a variable or a group of related variables over time, compared with a base period.
The normal period with which other periods are compared; its index is taken as 100.

sections.heading: 2. Wholesale price index, consumer price index and index of industrial production
sections.body_md:
The **wholesale price index** measures the change in the general price level of goods traded in **bulk**. As commonly taught, it is compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser, Ministry of Commerce and Industry.

The **consumer price index**, or **cost-of-living index**, measures the change in the **retail prices** of a **fixed basket** of goods and services consumed by a **defined group**. As commonly taught, there are indices for industrial workers, for agricultural labourers, and for rural, urban and combined households. It is used to adjust dearness allowance and wages.

The **index of industrial production** measures the change in the **volume** of industrial output (mining, manufacturing and electricity), so it is a quantity index. The **Sensex** is the stock market index of the Bombay Stock Exchange, based on thirty companies.

sections.body_md:
**Laspeyres:** Σp1q0 ÷ Σp0q0 × 100, with the **base-year** quantities as weights. It compares the cost of the base-year basket at current and at base prices.

**Paasche:** Σp1q1 ÷ Σp0q1 × 100, with the **current-year** quantities as weights. It compares the cost of the current-year basket at current and at base prices.

For the imagined Pinecrest Stationers, Σp0q0 = 500, Σp1q0 = 616, Σp0q1 = 1000 and Σp1q1 = 1212, so Laspeyres = 123.2 and Paasche = 121.2.

sections.heading: 7. Inflation, real wage and purchasing power
sections.body_md:
**Inflation** is a sustained rise in the general price level. Its rate between two years is **(I1 − I0) ÷ I0 × 100**, where I is a price index. A lower rate of inflation still means that prices are rising, only more slowly.

**Real wage = money wage ÷ consumer price index × 100.** When prices rise faster than the money wage, the real wage and the purchasing power fall. In the imagined Bhavnagar Colony the index is 100, 125, 130, 143, 150, 165; the rates of inflation are 25, 4, 10, 4.9, 10 per cent. A clerk's money wage of Rs 15000, 16900, 17160 gives real wages of Rs 12000, 13000, 12000.

The money wage adjusted for price changes, equal to the money wage divided by the consumer price index and multiplied by 100.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best defines an index number?

options.text_md: The simple arithmetic average of all the prices in an economy
A statistical device that measures the relative change in a variable or a group of related variables over time, compared with a base period
The total value of all goods produced in a year
The difference between the highest and the lowest price in a market

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A statistical device that measures the relative change in a variable or a group of related variables over time, compared with a base period. An index number shows how a variable, or a group of related variables, has changed relative to a base period. It is not a plain average, a total of output value or a range of prices.

questions.stem_md: In the usual convention, the value of an index number in its base period is taken as
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 100. The base period is the reference point, and its index is set at 100, so that a later value above 100 shows a rise and a value below 100 shows a fall.

questions.stem_md: The statistician of the imagined Bhavnagar Colony Welfare Society must choose a base year for the colony's consumer price index. Which choice is most sensible?

options.text_md: A normal year, free of unusual events such as a long shortage or a flood
The year in which prices were highest, so that every later index is below 100
A year chosen at random from the last century
The year with the most unusual events, to show how prices react

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A normal year, free of unusual events such as a long shortage or a flood. A base year should be a normal one, so that the comparison is not distorted by an abnormal event. A year of extreme prices or of unusual events would make every later comparison misleading.

questions.stem_md: The wholesale price index measures the change in

options.text_md: the retail prices paid by a family of industrial workers
the volume of industrial output
the general price level of goods traded in bulk
the share prices of thirty companies

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the general price level of goods traded in bulk. The wholesale price index follows the prices of goods traded in bulk. Retail prices belong to the consumer price index, output volume to the index of industrial production and share prices to the Sensex.

questions.stem_md: The consumer price index differs from the wholesale price index mainly because it

options.text_md: tracks only the prices of machines and raw materials
measures the quantity of goods produced by factories
tracks retail prices of a fixed basket of goods and services consumed by a defined group
measures the number of people employed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** tracks retail prices of a fixed basket of goods and services consumed by a defined group. The consumer price index follows retail prices of a fixed basket bought by a defined group of consumers, so it reflects the cost of living of that group. The other options describe quantities or capital goods, not retail prices.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is commonly named as a kind of consumer price index?

options.text_md: The index for agricultural labourers
The index for share brokers
The index of coal output
The index of retail shops opened

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The index for agricultural labourers. As commonly taught, consumer price indices are compiled for industrial workers, for agricultural labourers, and for rural, urban and combined populations. A share-broker index, a coal output index or a shop-count index is not a consumer price index.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Sundaram Textile Works revises the dearness allowance of its employees each half year. Which index would it most naturally use?

options.text_md: The index of industrial production
The Sensex
The index of mining output
The consumer price index

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The consumer price index. Dearness allowance is meant to protect the purchasing power of wages against a rise in the cost of living, which the consumer price index measures. Output indices and a share index say nothing of what workers pay for goods.

questions.stem_md: The index of industrial production measures the change in

options.text_md: the retail price of manufactured goods
the volume of industrial output, such as mining, manufacturing and electricity
the wages of factory workers
the profits of listed companies

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the volume of industrial output, such as mining, manufacturing and electricity. The index of industrial production follows the physical volume of output of industries such as mining, manufacturing and electricity. It is a quantity index, not a price index.

questions.stem_md: A planner at the imagined Rivergate Industrial Estate wants to know whether the quantity of goods made there has risen over three years, whatever has happened to prices. The best index is

options.text_md: an index of industrial production, which measures volume
a wholesale price index, which measures bulk prices
a consumer price index, which measures retail prices
the Sensex, which measures share prices

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** an index of industrial production, which measures volume. The question is about the quantity produced, so a volume index of production is needed. The other three are price indices and would change even if output stayed the same.

questions.stem_md: A trade union of the imagined Bhavnagar Colony Cooperative Society wants to show that its members' cost of living has risen faster than their pay. Which index is the most relevant evidence?

options.text_md: The index of industrial production
The consumer price index of the group of workers concerned
The wholesale price index of raw materials
The Sensex

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The consumer price index of the group of workers concerned. The union is concerned with what its members pay in shops, which the consumer price index for the relevant group measures. The other indices describe output, bulk prices or share prices.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is NOT a use of index numbers?

options.text_md: Measuring the rate of inflation
Deflating money values to real terms
Fixing the exact price of every good in a shop
Adjusting wages and allowances

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Fixing the exact price of every good in a shop. Index numbers show changes over time; they do not fix the price of any good. Measuring inflation, deflating money values and adjusting wages are standard uses.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined Madhupur Mill Colony, a family spends far more on food than on tea. If the consumer price index gave both items the same importance, the index would

options.text_md: be exact, because every item is equally important to every family
stay at 100 whatever the prices
measure output and not prices
misrepresent the cost of living, because a change in the price of food matters more to the family

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** misrepresent the cost of living, because a change in the price of food matters more to the family. Items matter in proportion to their share in the family's spending, so weights are needed. Equal importance would let a change in the price of tea count as much as a change in the price of food, which distorts the cost of living.

questions.stem_md: The retail price index of the imagined Bhavnagar Colony is 125 when the base year is 100. This shows that retail prices in the colony are, on average,

options.text_md: 125 per cent higher than in the base year
25 per cent lower than in the base year
the same as in the base year
25 per cent higher than in the base year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 25 per cent higher than in the base year. An index of 125 against a base of 100 means a rise of 25 points on 100, that is 25 per cent. It is not 125 per cent higher, and prices are not lower or unchanged.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Palsana Dairy Union finds that the total of the current prices of its inputs is Rs 475 against Rs 500 in the base year. Its simple aggregative price index is

options.text_md: 95, which shows that prices have risen by 5 per cent
5, which shows that prices have fallen
95, which shows that prices have fallen by 5 per cent
100, which shows no change

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 95, which shows that prices have fallen by 5 per cent. Index = 475 ÷ 500 × 100 = 95. A value below 100 shows a fall of 5 per cent. The other options misread either the value or its direction.

questions.stem_md: The simple aggregative price index for the current year is found by

options.text_md: multiplying the total of the current prices by the total of the base-year prices
dividing the total of the current prices by the total of the base-year prices and multiplying by 100
subtracting the base-year prices from the current prices and dividing by 100
adding the quantities bought and dividing by the number of items

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** dividing the total of the current prices by the total of the base-year prices and multiplying by 100. The formula is the total of current prices divided by the total of base-year prices, times 100. The other options do not give a ratio of price totals.

questions.stem_md: The main limitation of the simple aggregative method is that

options.text_md: the index depends on the units in which the prices of the items are quoted
it cannot be worked out when prices rise
it always gives a value of 100
it needs the quantities of every item

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the index depends on the units in which the prices of the items are quoted. The method adds up prices, so quoting one item per dozen or per piece changes the total and the index. It works for rising prices, does not always give 100 and needs no quantities.

questions.stem_md: In the Laspeyres method the weights are

options.text_md: the quantities of the current year
the quantities of the base year
the prices of the current year
equal for all items

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the quantities of the base year. The Laspeyres index prices the base-year basket at current and at base-year prices, so base-year quantities are its weights. Current-year quantities belong to the Paasche method.

questions.stem_md: The Paasche price index asks what

options.text_md: the base-year basket costs at current prices compared with its cost at base-year prices
the average of the price relatives is
the difference between the highest and the lowest price is
the current-year basket costs at current prices compared with its cost at base-year prices

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the current-year basket costs at current prices compared with its cost at base-year prices. The Paasche index compares the cost of the current-year quantities at current prices with their cost at base-year prices. Using the base-year basket is the Laspeyres idea.

questions.stem_md: As commonly taught, the consumer price index is computed as

options.text_md: a weighted average of price relatives, with weights from the family budget
a simple total of prices
the total of quantities produced
the highest price relative

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a weighted average of price relatives, with weights from the family budget. Price relatives are multiplied by family-budget weights, added, and divided by the total weight. A simple total of prices would ignore how much each item matters to the family.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined Bhavnagar Colony fair, the price of a shirt was Rs 60 in the base year and Rs 81 this year. Its price relative is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 135. Price relative = current price ÷ base price × 100 = 81 ÷ 60 × 100 = 135. Dividing the other way round, or taking a difference, does not give a relative.

questions.stem_md: Inflation is best described as

options.text_md: a single rise in the price of one good
a fall in the general price level
a sustained rise in the general price level
a rise in the volume of production

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a sustained rise in the general price level. Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, not a single change in one price. A fall in the general level is deflation, and output volume is a different matter.

questions.stem_md: The rate of inflation between two years, from a price index, is

options.text_md: the change in the index divided by the earlier index, multiplied by 100
the later index divided by 100
the sum of the two indices
the earlier index divided by the later index

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the change in the index divided by the earlier index, multiplied by 100. Rate of inflation = (later index − earlier index) ÷ earlier index × 100. The other expressions do not measure a percentage change.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined Lakshmi Weaving Cooperative, the money wage of a weaver rises by 6 per cent in a year while the consumer price index rises by 9 per cent. The real wage

options.text_md: rises, because the money wage rose
stays the same, because both rose
cannot be judged without the price of cloth
falls, because prices rose faster than the wage

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** falls, because prices rose faster than the wage. When prices rise faster than the money wage, the wage buys less, so the real wage falls. A rise in money wage does not raise the real wage unless it outpaces prices.

questions.stem_md: The consumer price index of the imagined Bhavnagar Colony stands at 125 against a base of 100. Measured in base-year rupees, the purchasing power of Rs 100 is about

options.text_md: Rs 125
Rs 80
Rs 25
Rs 100

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Rs 80. Purchasing power = 100 ÷ index × 100 = 100 ÷ 125 × 100 = Rs 80. When prices are higher than in the base year, a rupee buys less.

questions.stem_md: For the imagined Pinecrest Stationers, the Laspeyres index is 123.2 and the Paasche index is 121.2. A sensible reason for the Laspeyres value being higher is that

options.text_md: in the current year buyers bought less of the items whose prices rose most, which the base-year weights do not show
the Paasche method always ignores prices
the Laspeyres method uses current-year quantities
prices did not change

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** in the current year buyers bought less of the items whose prices rose most, which the base-year weights do not show. Base-year weights keep the earlier buying pattern, while current-year weights reflect the shift away from items that became dearer. In the data the quantity of the notebook fell from 16 to 12. The Paasche method does use prices, Laspeyres uses base-year quantities, and prices did change.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The index number of the base period is taken as 100.

**Reason (R):** The base period is the reference with which the other periods are compared.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A. Since every other period is compared with the base, its own index is set at the convenient value of 100.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The simple aggregative index changes if the unit of one item is changed from a dozen to a piece.

**Reason (R):** The method adds prices that are quoted in different units.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A. A change of unit alters the price of that item and so the total, which is why the method is sensitive to units.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The index of industrial production measures the change in the prices of industrial goods.

**Reason (R):** It covers industries such as mining, manufacturing and electricity.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: the index measures the volume of output, not prices. R is true: those industries are covered.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The consumer price index tracks the retail prices of a basket bought by a defined group.

**Reason (R):** The wholesale price index tracks the prices of goods traded in bulk.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but the second does not explain the first. They describe two different indices.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An index of 110 against a base of 100 shows that prices have risen by 10 per cent.

**Reason (R):** The base period of an index number is always taken as 0.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: 110 is 10 per cent above 100. R is false, since the base period is taken as 100, not 0.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The wholesale price index records the retail prices paid by a family at the corner shop of the imagined Bhavnagar Colony.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The wholesale price index records the prices of goods traded in bulk. Retail prices belong to the consumer price index.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the imagined Bhavnagar Colony the index rises from 143 to 150, so the rate of inflation is 4.9 per cent, lower than the 10 per cent of the previous year. This shows that prices are now falling.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** A lower rate of inflation means prices are still rising, only more slowly. Prices fall only when the index itself falls.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Paasche index uses the quantities of the current year as weights.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** In the Paasche method the weights are current-year quantities; Laspeyres uses base-year quantities.

questions.stem_md: A price relative is the price of the current year divided by the price of the ___ year, multiplied by 100.
questions.solution_md: A price relative compares the current price with the base-year price.

questions.stem_md: Real wage is the money wage divided by the ___ and multiplied by 100.
questions.solution_md: Dividing the money wage by the consumer price index and multiplying by 100 gives the real wage.

questions.stem_md: Match each index with what it measures.

options.text_md: Wholesale price index
Consumer price index
Index of industrial production
Sensex

match_right.text_md: Change in retail prices of a basket consumed by a defined group
Movement of the share prices of thirty companies of the Bombay Stock Exchange
Change in the general price level of goods traded in bulk
Change in the volume of output of mining, manufacturing and electricity

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Each index has its own subject: bulk prices, retail prices of a basket, volume of industrial output, and share prices.

questions.stem_md: Match each method of constructing a price index with its description.

options.text_md: Simple aggregative method
Simple average of price relatives
Laspeyres method
Paasche method

match_right.text_md: Weights are the quantities of the current year
Total of current prices divided by total of base-year prices, times 100
Weights are the quantities of the base year
Mean of the price relatives of the items

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). The first two methods are unweighted, and the last two are weighted aggregative methods that differ in the year whose quantities are used.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps of constructing a consumer price index by the weighted average of price relatives for the imagined Madhupur Mill Colony.

options.text_md: Divide the total by the sum of the weights
Multiply each relative by its weight from the family budget
Add the products to get the total of relatives times weights
Find the price relative of each item or group

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (b) → (c) → (a). The relatives come first, then they are weighted, the weighted figures are added, and the division by the total weight comes last.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps of working out a Laspeyres index for the imagined Shanti Canteen in a sensible order.

options.text_md: Multiply the ratio by 100
Divide the cost at current prices by the cost at base-year prices
Find the cost of the base-year quantities at current prices and at base-year prices
Write down the base-year quantities as weights

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (c) → (b) → (a). The weights are fixed first, the two costs are found, the ratio of costs is formed and finally scaled by 100.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Sunrise Bakery noted the prices of four inputs in the base year and this year: flour (kg) Rs 40 then Rs 44; sugar (kg) Rs 40 then Rs 46; butter (kg) Rs 400 then Rs 480; eggs (dozen) Rs 60 then Rs 78. Find the simple aggregative price index for this year.

For the Sunrise Bakery inputs, flour (kg) Rs 40 then Rs 44; sugar (kg) Rs 40 then Rs 46; butter (kg) Rs 400 then Rs 480; eggs (dozen) Rs 60 then Rs 78, find the index by the simple average of price relatives.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The relatives are 110, 115, 120, 130.
Step 2: Their sum is 475.
Step 3: Index = 475 ÷ 4 = 118.75.

questions.stem_md: An imagined household of Bhavnagar Colony noted its prices (Rs, base year then current year): wheat flour (kg) Rs 40 then Rs 50; pulses (kg) Rs 100 then Rs 120; milk (litre) Rs 60 then Rs 75; cooking oil (litre) Rs 120 then Rs 150; tea (pack) Rs 80 then Rs 105. Find the price index by the simple average of price relatives, correct to two decimals.

The imagined Pinecrest Stationers sold 16, 2, 3, 2 units of notebook, pen, geometry box, file folder respectively in the base term, at base prices of Rs 20, 10, 50, 5; the current prices are Rs 25, 12, 60, 6. Find the Laspeyres price index.

In the current term the imagined Pinecrest Stationers sold 12, 3, 13, 16 units of notebook, pen, geometry box, file folder respectively. The base prices are Rs 20, 10, 50, 5 and the current prices are Rs 25, 12, 60, 6. Find the Paasche price index.

At the imagined Shanti Canteen the base-year prices of a meal plate, a sandwich and a fruit juice were Rs 50, 30, 20 and the current prices are Rs 60, 36, 28. The base-year sales were 16, 5, 15 units a day. Find the Laspeyres index.

Find the consumer price index by the weighted average of price relatives.

The consumer price index of the imagined Bhavnagar Colony was 130 in Year 2 and 143 in Year 3. Find the rate of inflation in Year 3.

questions.stem_md: The price index of the imagined Bhavnagar Colony was 143 in Year 3 and 150 in Year 4. Find the rate of inflation in Year 4, correct to two decimals.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Change in the index = 150 − 143 = 7.
Step 2: Rate = 7 ÷ 143 × 100 = 4.9 per cent.

questions.stem_md: An imagined clerk of the Bhavnagar Colony Cooperative Society earned Rs 16900 a month in Year 2, when the consumer price index was 130. Find the real wage.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Real wage = money wage ÷ index × 100.
Step 2: 16900 ÷ 130 × 100 = 13000 rupees.

questions.stem_md: An imagined employee of the Sundaram Textile Works earns Rs 24000 a month when the consumer price index is 125. The index rises to 150. What monthly pay would keep the real wage unchanged?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Real wage now = 24000 ÷ 125 × 100 = 19200.
Step 2: Pay needed = 19200 × 150 ÷ 100 = 28800 rupees.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Kaushal Printers had sales of Rs 286 lakh in Year 2, when the consumer price index of its town was 130. Express the sales in terms of base-year prices (real sales).
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Real value = money value ÷ index × 100.
Step 2: 286 ÷ 130 × 100 = 220 Rs lakh.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Palsana Dairy Union paid Rs 250 for a set of inputs in the base year. Its simple aggregative price index is now 128. Find the total of the current prices of the same set.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Index = Σp1 ÷ Σp0 × 100, so Σp1 = index × Σp0 ÷ 100.
Step 2: Σp1 = 128 × 250 ÷ 100 = 320 rupees.

questions.stem_md: Define an index number and say what is meant by the base period.
questions.solution_md: Definition; base period.

answer.model_answer_md: An **index number** is a statistical device that measures the relative change in a variable or a group of related variables over time. The **base period** is the period with which other periods are compared; its index is taken as **100**.

marking_scheme.step: Base period and its value of 100

questions.stem_md: What does the wholesale price index measure, and which office compiles it, as commonly taught?
questions.solution_md: What it measures; who compiles it.

answer.model_answer_md: This index tracks how the **general price level of goods sold in bulk** changes over time. The compiler, as commonly taught, is the **Office of the Economic Adviser** in the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.

marking_scheme.step: Change in the general price level of goods traded in bulk
Office of the Economic Adviser, Ministry of Commerce and Industry

questions.stem_md: Give two uses of the consumer price index.
questions.solution_md: Any two uses.

answer.model_answer_md: The consumer price index is used to **measure the cost of living and inflation** faced by a group of consumers, and to **adjust wages and dearness allowance** so that workers keep their purchasing power.

questions.stem_md: How does the index of industrial production differ from the consumer price index in what it measures?
questions.solution_md: Volume against retail price.

answer.model_answer_md: The index of industrial production measures the change in the **volume of output** of mining, manufacturing and electricity, so it is a **quantity** index. The consumer price index measures the change in the **retail prices** paid by consumers, so it is a **price** index.

questions.stem_md: What is the Sensex? Name the body whose shares it follows.
questions.solution_md: Sensex as the Bombay Stock Exchange index of thirty companies.

answer.model_answer_md: It is the **share-market index** of the **Bombay Stock Exchange**. It is built on the share prices of **thirty companies** listed there, and so shows the general movement of the market.

questions.stem_md: Why should the base year of a price index be a normal year? Illustrate with an imagined case from Bhavnagar Colony.
questions.solution_md: Base as yardstick; distortion by an abnormal year.

answer.model_answer_md: A base year is the yardstick for every later comparison, so an abnormal year would distort it. If the imagined colony chose a year of acute shortage, when prices were unusually high, every later index would look **lower** than the real change in prices.

marking_scheme.step: Base is the yardstick for comparison

questions.stem_md: State one limitation of the simple aggregative method and one way of overcoming it.
questions.solution_md: Unit dependence; relatives or weights.

answer.model_answer_md: The simple aggregative index depends on the **units** in which prices are quoted, for example per dozen or per piece. It is overcome by using **price relatives**, which are pure numbers, or by using **weights**.

questions.stem_md: Define inflation and write the formula for its rate from a price index.
questions.solution_md: Definition and formula.

answer.model_answer_md: **Inflation** is a sustained rise in the general price level, not a one-time rise in a single price. Its rate between two years is **(later index − earlier index) ÷ earlier index × 100**, expressed as a per cent.

questions.stem_md: Why can a rise in the money wage still leave a worker worse off? Name the measure that corrects for this.
questions.solution_md: Prices outpacing wages; real wage.

answer.model_answer_md: If the consumer price index rises faster than the money wage, the wage buys less, so the **purchasing power** falls. The measure that corrects for this is the **real wage**, equal to the money wage divided by the consumer price index and multiplied by 100.

marking_scheme.step: Prices rising faster than the wage lowers purchasing power

questions.stem_md: A kilogram of rice in the imagined Mahuva market cost Rs 60 in the base year and costs Rs 81 now. Find its price relative and say what it shows.
questions.solution_md: Relative 135; a rise of 35 per cent.

answer.model_answer_md: Price relative = 81 ÷ 60 × 100 = **135**. It shows that the price is 35 per cent higher than in the base year.

marking_scheme.step: Interpretation as a rise over the base

questions.stem_md: State any three issues to be considered in constructing an index number.
questions.solution_md: Any three of purpose, base year, items, price quotations, weights and formula.

answer.model_answer_md: First, the **purpose** of the index decides what is measured and for whom. Second, the **base year** should be normal. Third, the **items** and their **price quotations**, wholesale or retail, must suit the purpose. Weights and the choice of the formula are also settled before the index is built.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish the Laspeyres index from the Paasche index.
questions.solution_md: Weights, the basket compared, data needed.

answer.model_answer_md: The **Laspeyres** index uses the **base-year quantities** as weights: it compares the cost of the base-year basket at current and at base prices. The **Paasche** index uses the **current-year quantities**: it compares the cost of the current basket at current and at base prices. Laspeyres needs quantities only once, while Paasche needs fresh quantities every year.

questions.stem_md: Describe the steps in constructing a consumer price index from a family budget.
questions.solution_md: Relatives; weighting and adding; division by the total weight.

answer.model_answer_md: First find the **price relative** of each item as current price over base price times 100. Then multiply each relative by its **weight**, taken from the family budget, and add the products. Finally divide by the **total of the weights** to get the index.

questions.stem_md: Prices of the imagined Sunrise Bakery were flour (kg) Rs 40 then Rs 44; sugar (kg) Rs 40 then Rs 46; butter (kg) Rs 400 then Rs 480; eggs (dozen) Rs 60 then Rs 78. The same prices are now quoted per 100 g of butter and per piece of eggs: flour (kg) Rs 40 then Rs 44; sugar (kg) Rs 40 then Rs 46; butter (100 g) Rs 40 then Rs 48; eggs (piece) Rs 5 then Rs 6.5. Find the simple aggregative index for both and say what the difference shows.
questions.solution_md: 120 and 115.6: dependence on units.

answer.model_answer_md: First set (butter per kg, eggs per dozen): Σp0 = 540 and Σp1 = 648, so the index is 648 ÷ 540 × 100 = **120**. Second set (butter per 100 g, eggs per piece): Σp0 = 125 and Σp1 = 144.5, so the index is 144.5 ÷ 125 × 100 = **115.6**. The price movements are identical, yet the indices differ, so the simple aggregative method depends on the units in which prices are quoted.

questions.stem_md: The price relatives of five groups for a worker family of the imagined Madhupur Mill Colony are food 130, housing 110, clothing 120, fuel and light 150, other items 100, with base-year monthly spending (Rs) 5000, 2500, 1000, 1000, 500 used as weights. Find the consumer price index.
questions.solution_md: Index 124.5.

answer.model_answer_md: Step 1: multiply each relative by its weight to get RW: 130×5000 = 650000; 110×2500 = 275000; 120×1000 = 120000; 150×1000 = 150000; 100×500 = 50000. Step 2: add them, so ΣRW = 1245000, and add the weights, so ΣW = 10000. Step 3: Index = 1245000 ÷ 10000 = **124.5**. The cost of living of these families is 24.5 per cent above the base year.

questions.stem_md: A worker of the imagined Ashoka Mess earned Rs 20000 a month when the consumer price index was 125, and Rs 21600 when it was 150. Find the real wage each time and the percentage change in it.
questions.solution_md: Real wages 16000 and 14400; fall of 10 per cent.

answer.model_answer_md: The real wage is the money wage divided by the index, times 100. Before: 20000 ÷ 125 × 100 = **16000** rupees. After: 21600 ÷ 150 × 100 = **14400** rupees. The fall is 16000 − 14400 = 1600 rupees, which is 1600 ÷ 16000 × 100 = **10 per cent**. The worker is worse off in real terms although the money wage rose.

questions.stem_md: Explain the wholesale price index, the consumer price index and the index of industrial production, saying what each measures.
questions.solution_md: Meaning, coverage and use of each of the three indices.

answer.model_answer_md: The **wholesale price index** measures the change in the general price level of goods traded in bulk, and is compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser, Ministry of Commerce and Industry. The **consumer price index**, or cost-of-living index, measures the change in the retail prices of a fixed basket of goods and services consumed by a defined group, such as industrial workers, agricultural labourers, or rural and urban households; it is used to adjust wages and dearness allowance. The **index of industrial production** measures the change in the volume of output of mining, manufacturing and electricity, so it is a quantity index and not a price index.

questions.stem_md: Explain the main uses of index numbers, with an imagined illustration for each.
questions.solution_md: Five uses with illustrations.

answer.model_answer_md: Index numbers **measure inflation**: a rise in the consumer price index of the imagined Bhavnagar Colony shows how fast prices rise. They **adjust wages and allowances**, as when an employer revises dearness allowance. They **deflate money values to real terms**, so that sales of a firm can be compared at base-year prices. They guide **policy-making**, since planners watch price and output indices. They also **compare performance over time**, as an output index shows whether a factory grows.

questions.stem_md: Discuss the issues that arise in constructing a consumer price index for the workers of the imagined Madhupur Mill Colony.
questions.solution_md: Purpose, base year, items, price quotations, weights and formula applied to the mill colony.

answer.model_answer_md: The **purpose** decides the group and what is to be measured: here the cost of living of mill workers. The **base year** should be normal, not one of shortage. The **items** must be those the workers actually buy. **Price quotations** must be retail prices, since workers buy at shops, not wholesale. **Weights** from the workers' family budget show the importance of each item, and a suitable **formula**, such as the weighted average of price relatives, must be chosen.

questions.stem_md: Compare the simple aggregative method, the simple average of price relatives, and the weighted aggregative methods of constructing a price index.
questions.solution_md: Features and limits of the four methods.

answer.model_answer_md: The **simple aggregative** index divides the total of current prices by the total of base prices; it is easy but depends on the units of the items. The **simple average of price relatives** is free of units because each relative is a ratio, but it treats every item as equally important. The **weighted aggregative** methods use quantities as weights: **Laspeyres** takes the base-year quantities and **Paasche** the current-year quantities. They show the importance of each item, though they need quantity data.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Tulsi Juice Bar sold 20, 6, 6 glasses of lemon, mango, sugarcane juice in the base week and 15, 14, 6 glasses in the current week. Prices (Rs a glass) were 8, 15, 25 in the base week and 10, 18, 30 now. Find the Laspeyres and the Paasche price indices.
questions.solution_md: Laspeyres 122; Paasche 121.25.

answer.model_answer_md: Laspeyres uses the base-week glasses as weights: Σp0q0 = 8×20 + 15×6 + 25×6 = 400, and Σp1q0 = 10×20 + 18×6 + 30×6 = 488. Index = Σp1q0 ÷ Σp0q0 × 100 = 488 ÷ 400 × 100 = **122**. Paasche uses the current-week glasses: Σp0q1 = 8×15 + 15×14 + 25×6 = 480, and Σp1q1 = 10×15 + 18×14 + 30×6 = 582. Index = 582 ÷ 480 × 100 = **121.25**. The Laspeyres value is higher because buyers shifted toward lemon, the cheapest juice.

questions.stem_md: An imagined family of Bhavnagar Colony has budget weights 30, 10, 20, 15, 10, 15 for wheat flour (kg), cooking oil (litre), milk (litre), gas cylinder, bus fare (trip), school notebooks (set), with base and current prices (Rs) 30 and 36; 80 and 100; 40 and 46; 800 and 880; 20 and 30; 40 and 44. Find the consumer price index. If it was 119.5 in the current year and rises to 131.45 in the next, find the rate of inflation for the next year.
questions.solution_md: Index 119.5; inflation 10 per cent.

answer.model_answer_md: Step 1: the price relatives are 120, 125, 115, 110, 150, 110. Step 2: multiplying each by its weight gives RW = 3600, 1250, 2300, 1650, 1500, 1650, so ΣRW = 11950, while ΣW = 100. Step 3: Index = ΣRW ÷ ΣW = 11950 ÷ 100 = **119.5**. Step 4: the rate of inflation is (later index − earlier index) ÷ earlier index × 100 = (131.45 − 119.5) ÷ 119.5 × 100 = **10 per cent**. Prices of the family's basket are therefore rising by this rate in the next year.
